concepts.primary_text:
I quit smoking in October of 2019 so I would stop getting chest infections.

By February of 2021, I was sitting on an exam table in the urgent care on Gloucester Crossing with pneumonia for the second winter in a row.

I was 49 years old.

I run a commercial lobster boat out of Gloucester, Massachusetts.

If you have ever worked the North Shore in January, you know what winter on the water is like.

You are down at the dock at 4:30 in the morning.

The deck has a thin skin of frozen salt spray.

The wind howls out of the northeast off Cape Ann, cutting straight through your bibs.

You haul 800 traps a day in six-foot swells, stacking wire gear, banding claws, breathing diesel fumes and freezing ocean mist.

It is hard work on a good day.

If your lungs go down, you are done.

That was why I quit smoking in 2019.

I went cold turkey after twenty-four years of a pack a day.

I did it for my lungs.

I started running three miles along Western Avenue every week.

I took vitamin C and ate clean.

I did everything right.

And then, every winter like clockwork, my chest gave out.

In December of 2019, it was a hacking cough that turned into severe bronchitis.

In January of 2021, my fever spiked to 102.4, my ribs ached, and I ended up flat on my back with bacterial pneumonia.

I missed thirteen days during peak holiday prices.

When winter lobster is bringing nine dollars a pound at the dock, sitting on the couch coughing up thick yellow gunk means burning through your mortgage money.

I sat in my truck in the harbor parking lot for twenty minutes staring at the steering wheel.

My sternman, a 26-year-old kid who smokes a pack of Camels on every trip, was out there pulling traps in thirty-knot winds without a runny nose.

And here I was, the guy who ran three miles before sunrise, wheezing into an inhaler.

I thought I was just unlucky.

Then my wife Colleen sat down at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon.

She had an accordion folder out with four years of our medical co-pays and pharmacy receipts.

She tapped her glasses against the table and looked right at me.

"Brendan, look at these dates."

From 2014 to 2019, I did not have a single urgent care visit for my chest.

Not one antibiotic prescription.

Then she slid a dental receipt across the table from November 12, 2019.

It was for my hard acrylic night guard.

My dentist had made it for me because twenty-five years of clenching my jaw through nor'easters had worn my back molars down to the dentin.

My first trip to urgent care for a chest infection was on January 4, 2020.

Almost six weeks after I started wearing that night guard.

Every single winter illness over the next three years happened between December and March, right in the middle of night guard season.

Everyone gives you the standard winter fisherman advice:

Drink hot black tea before you leave the harbor.

Wear double-layered merino wool under your bibs.

Take vitamin D3 every morning.

Keep your head dry when the sea kicks up.

Nobody ever talks about the five-inch piece of hard acrylic you shove into your mouth right before you close your eyes.

Two days later, I went back to the clinic for a chest x-ray.

My old deckhand Neil has a wife named Lauren who works there as a respiratory therapist.

She was standing at the counter talking to Dr. Hayes when I walked in.

I had my plastic night guard case in my jacket pocket, and when I pulled my truck keys out, the case fell and hit the floor.

Lauren looked at it.

"Brendan, what is that?"

"My night guard," I said. "For teeth grinding."

"How do you clean it?"

"I rinse it in the sink under hot tap water in the morning. Brush it with my toothbrush sometimes. Once a week I drop a blue tablet in a cup."

Lauren did not even smile.

She looked at Dr. Hayes, and Dr. Hayes shook his head.

"Brendan," Dr. Hayes said, "have you ever heard of aspiration pneumonia?"

"Wait, what does that even mean?" I asked.

Dr. Hayes pointed at the little plastic case.

"To your eye, that acrylic looks smooth and solid. But under a laboratory microscope, dental acrylic is full of microscopic pores, micro-fissures, and tiny scratches."

He told me that every night you wear it, your mouth bacteria, yeast, and saliva seep deep into those pores.

Then you take it out in the morning, give it a quick five-second splash under the tap, and snap it shut inside a dark, damp plastic case.

That closed case sits on your bathroom counter for sixteen hours at room temperature.

It is a warm incubator.

The bacteria and mold do not wash off with water.

They multiply inside the microscopic pores all day long.

And then at night, you put that bacteria-soaked piece of plastic right back over your teeth.

For eight hours straight, you swallow saliva and breathe shallowly over that colony.

When you sleep, your cough and swallow reflexes relax.

Micro-droplets of saliva carrying that live bacterial biofilm slip straight past your vocal cords and drain down into your bronchial tubes and your lungs.

It is called aspiration.

And your lungs are warm, dark, and moist, which means those mouth germs take root immediately.

I stood there in the clinic hallway staring at the linoleum floor.

Later on, I looked up the actual clinical research.

A 2015 study by Iinuma and colleagues in the Journal of Dental Research followed 524 people over three years.

They found that people who slept with oral appliances in their mouths had more than double the risk of pneumonia compared to those who did not.

They also had significantly more bacterial plaque and Candida yeast.

Another study in 2016 by O'Donnell in the Journal of Prosthodontics found that pneumonia-causing germs were actively colonizing 64% of the oral appliances they sampled.

Almost two-thirds of those appliances were carrying pathogens known to cause lung infections.

And I had been soaking mine in spit, sealing it in a plastic box, and breathing over it every single night.

I threw the plastic case onto the counter and paced the kitchen.

I had spent thousands on healthy food, running shoes, and gym visits, while shoving a concentrated ball of bacteria into my mouth seven nights a week.

I went home determined to clean it.

First, I scrubbed it with my regular soft toothbrush and paste.

The toothpaste cost five dollars.

It smelled like mint, but within two days the acrylic was getting cloudier.

Lauren told me that regular toothpaste contains microscopic abrasives made for enamel.

On acrylic, toothpaste gouges microscopic scratches into the surface, creating deeper trenches for yellow bacteria and white film to hide.

Next, I bought blue fizzing cleaning tablets from the grocery store.

That was eighteen dollars a month, or over two hundred dollars a year.

They bubbled in a cup and made my bathroom smell like pool chlorine.

The persulfates in those tablets burned my tongue in the morning.

In fact, the FDA had issued a public health notice about allergic reactions to persulfates in cleansers back in 2008.

Worst of all, the tablets only bleached the surface.

Underneath, the night guard still had a sour, stale smell, and the yellow stains around the molar channels kept getting darker.

Then I bought one of those $35 generic vibrating cleaning pods off Amazon.

It felt like a cheap plastic toy.

It buzzed loudly on the counter, but the water barely moved.

After nineteen days, the motor died completely.

I found out that in a 90-day lab test comparing seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six out of seven pods left live bacterial biofilm active on appliances overnight.

They simply lacked the power to penetrate the pores.

A week later, Neil walked down our dock with a plain cardboard box under his arm.

He set it on the engine hatch of my boat.

"Lauren ordered this for you," he said. "She uses it on her own night guard. Stop buying junk."

Inside was the DentalPULSE Pod.

It was an ultrasonic cleaner specifically engineered for dental appliances like night guards, retainers, and dentures.

The retail price was $99.95.

I stood on the deck and did the math.

My urgent care co-pay was $185.

My prescriptions were $68.

And losing two weeks during winter hauling had cost me over $7,500 in lost income.

Paying $99.95 once for a clinical-grade ultrasonic cleaner was not an expense.

It was the cheapest insurance policy I had ever bought.

Here is why the DentalPULSE Pod is completely different from anything else:

First, it uses a medical-grade 42,000 Hz ultrasonic transducer.

That means it creates 42,000 microscopic sound-wave implosions every second.

Those tiny cavitation bubbles blast into every microscopic pore and scratch in the acrylic, ripping biofilm, yellow stains, and trapped gunk out from the inside.

Second, it pairs that ultrasonic power with built-in medical-grade UV-C light.

While the ultrasonic waves scrub the physical debris, the UV-C light attacks the DNA of the bacteria, eliminating 99.9% of bacteria in one 5-minute cycle.

You do not have to wait thirty minutes or soak it all night. It runs for five minutes, and it shuts off.

Third, it has a surgical-grade stainless steel tank and runs on plain tap water.

You do not need blue chemical tablets or persulfates.

And there are no monthly subscriptions to buy.

Just cold water from the tap, one push of the button, and five minutes later it shuts off automatically.

That night, I took my cloudy, yellow-tinged night guard and set it in the stainless steel basin.

I filled it with tap water and pressed the button.

A gentle hum started, and the UV-C light clicked on.

Five minutes later, the cycle finished.

When I lifted the lid, I pulled my head back.

The water was murky, yellowish-brown, with tiny flakes of grey biofilm floating on the surface.

That brown sludge had been living inside my night guard while I slept.

I dumped the dirty water, rinsed the guard, and put it in my mouth.

It tasted like clean water.

No stale plastic taste. No sour tang. No chemical chlorine flavor from tablets.

By day three, the slick, slimy coating was completely gone.

When I ran my tongue across the inside of the guard, it felt smooth and clean like a polished piece of glass.

By week two, the stubborn white film that had lived in the crevices around my molars was completely stripped away.

The guard looked clear again, not milky.

It will not magically restore set-in yellow plastic from years ago back to factory new, but it stops it turning yellow any further and leaves it completely free of white film and odor.

Then came the real test: December.

Winter hit Massachusetts hard.

The temperature on the harbor dropped to fourteen degrees.

The sea spray froze to our wheelhouse windows.

I worked fourteen-hour days on the deck, hauling traps, breathing freezing salt mist and heavy diesel exhaust.

And my chest stayed completely clear.

I did not cough up yellow phlegm once.

My breathing was clear, and my fever stayed away.

For the first winter in four years, I did not miss a single tide.

My crew worked every weather window, and my boat made every single run of the season.

I blame that dirty, bacteria-loaded night guard for every single winter infection I suffered between 2019 and 2022.

If you wear a night guard, retainer, aligner, or dentures, you cannot clean it with a toothbrush or a fizzing tablet.

You need an ultrasonic cleaner that actually penetrates the pores.

Right now, go into your bathroom and pick up your night guard case.

Pop the latch.

Hold the guard up against the bathroom window.

Run your thumbnail hard along the inside groove where your back molars sit.

If you see a cloudy, yellowish haze through the acrylic, I have bad news.

Or if a thin, milky smear comes off on your nail.

That is not normal aging.

And that is definitely not clean.

That is live bacterial biofilm living inside the tiny pores of your night guard.

And if you have been dropping it into a glass of blue bubbling retainer tablets every morning like I did, you are making it worse.

You are slowly destroying your $650 night guard.

I should have known better.

I am a 41-year-old licensed vet tech at an animal hospital on Central Avenue in Albany, New York.

Five days a week, my job is dental cleanings on cats and dogs.

When a dog comes into our clinic with heavy tartar, brown stains, and red gums, do you know what we use?

We do not scrub their teeth with a plastic toothbrush.

We do not soak their jaws in a bowl of fizzy mint water.

I pick up a surgical ultrasonic scaler that vibrates at 40,000 cycles a second.

The sound waves create tiny bubbles in a stream of water.

Those tiny bubbles implode against the teeth.

They blast away rock-hard calculus, yellow stains, and bacteria without scratching the enamel.

I have done that on hundreds of animals for over a decade.

I understand the physics of ultrasonic cleaning with my eyes closed.

And yet, for over two years, I did something completely backwards.

Every morning, I took my own custom hard acrylic night guard out of my mouth.

I gave it a splash of tap water.

Then I dropped it into a coffee mug with a blue retainer cleaning tablet.

I watched the little blue bubbles fizz.

It smelled like wintergreen and chlorine.

I thought I was taking great care of it.

I got that night guard back in the fall of 2022.

Severe stress grinding was giving me morning tension headaches.

My dentist had custom-molded it out of hard dental plastic.

It cost me $650 out of pocket.

The dental assistant handed me sample cleaning tablets.

She told me to soak it every morning so it would not get smelly.

Wake up, take the guard out, drop it in a mug of water with a tablet.

Let it bubble while I got ready for work.

Rinse it, and lock it in the plastic case.

Within six months, I noticed the guard was losing its crystal-clear shine.

It looked foggy, milky, and cloudy.

Then a pale yellowish tint started setting into the molar pads.

I figured the tablets needed more time.

So I started leaving it in the cup for twelve hours while I was at work.

That was a huge mistake.

By month fourteen, the acrylic had turned completely chalky around the edges.

It felt dry and rough against my tongue instead of smooth.

And then, on a Tuesday morning last October, disaster hit.

I took the guard out of the blue tablet water.

I went to dry it with a paper towel.

I heard a sharp snap.

A clean fracture ran right down the front ridge between my two front teeth.

The acrylic had snapped clean in half.

I brought the two broken pieces to my dentist on Friday, assuming there had to be a warranty.

My dentist took one look at the chalky, discolored plastic.

He asked me how I had been cleaning it.

I told him I soaked it in retainer cleaning tablets every single morning.

He sighed and shook his head.

"Those effervescent tablets contain persulfates and strong oxidizers," he told me.

"Over time, they leach the plasticizers right out of hard acrylic. They make the appliance brittle and porous. That is why it cracked."

Then he handed me the bill for a replacement: another $650.

I walked out to my car and threw the estimate onto the passenger seat.

The next morning at the clinic, I was sitting in the breakroom venting to Dr. Morrison, one of our senior veterinarians.

I had the two broken pieces in a plastic bag on the table.

Dr. Morrison picked up the bag.

She held it up to the fluorescent light and started laughing.

"Christine," she said, "you spend forty hours a week running an ultrasonic scaler on dog teeth. Why on earth were you soaking your own mouth guard in grocery-store bleach tablets?"

The exact technology I used every day on dogs was what my own night guard needed all along.

Dental acrylic looks smooth.

Every night you grind your teeth, your saliva and mouth bacteria get forced deep into those pores.

Brushing with a regular toothbrush does nothing.

The bristles are way too fat to fit inside the pores.

And using toothpaste is worse.

Toothpaste has abrasives that create thousands of new microscopic scratches for bacteria to colonize.

Then people try retainer tablets or Polident.

Those tablets are mostly sodium bicarbonate, citric acid, and persulfates.

In fact, back in 2008, the FDA issued a public health notice warning about allergic reactions to persulfates in dental cleansers.

The bubbling you see is just surface fizz.

The chemical oxidizer bleaches the surface so it looks temporarily cleaner.

It cannot penetrate the microscopic pores where the bacteria live.

Even worse, the oxidizers weaken the molecular bonds of the acrylic.

They turn it chalky, brittle, and yellow over time until it cracks.

I went home and spent that evening looking into ultrasonic cleaners.

First, I tried a cheap $29 vibrating pod I found on a social media ad.

It was complete garbage.

It had a weak little motor that just shook the water like an electric toothbrush.

It had no real ultrasonic power.

It made an annoying buzzing sound, had no UV light, and the power cord stopped working on day seventeen.
